hld-feed-chat:0.prompt: In a news feed, what does fan-out on write (push model) mean?
options: When a user opens the app, the system queries all followees' posts and merges them
When a user posts, the post id is pushed into each follower's precomputed timeline, so reading a feed is a cheap lookup
Posts are written to every data center synchronously
Each follower's client polls the author's profile
hld-feed-chat:0.explanation: Push does the work at write time by inserting into followers' timelines (often Redis lists), making reads fast. Merging followees' posts at read time is fan-out on read (pull).

hld-feed-chat:0.prompt: Why does pure fan-out on write break down for celebrity accounts with 50 million followers?
options: Celebrities post less often, so their timelines go stale
Redis cannot store 50 million keys
A single post triggers 50 million timeline writes, creating a huge write spike and delivery lag, much of it for inactive followers
Followers cannot read posts from verified accounts
hld-feed-chat:0.explanation: Write amplification equals follower count: one celebrity post means tens of millions of inserts, delaying delivery and wasting work on users who never log in. Redis can hold that many keys; the problem is the burst of writes per post.

hld-feed-chat:0.prompt: What is the standard hybrid solution to the celebrity problem?
options: Push posts from normal users into followers' timelines; for celebrities, skip fan-out and merge their recent posts into the feed at read time
Pull every post at read time for all users
Limit celebrities to 1,000 followers
Push celebrity posts only to their most active followers and drop the rest
hld-feed-chat:0.explanation: The hybrid model keeps reads cheap for the common case (push) while avoiding massive write amplification for high-follower accounts (pull + merge at read). Dropping posts for less active followers would break correctness.

hld-feed-chat:0.prompt: An average user has 300 followers and the system sees 6,000 new posts/second with pure fan-out on write. Roughly how many timeline inserts per second is that?
options: 18 million
1.8 million
hld-feed-chat:0.explanation: 6,000 posts/s × 300 followers = 1,800,000 timeline inserts per second. This kind of estimate shows why fan-out workers must be horizontally scaled and why celebrity accounts (far above average) are handled separately.

hld-feed-chat:0.prompt: Fan-out on read (pull) is chosen for a system. What is its main downside?
options: Posts take longer to be written
Feed reads become expensive: each request must fetch and merge recent posts from every followee, which is slow for users who follow thousands of accounts
It stores many more copies of each post
Users can't see posts from people they follow
hld-feed-chat:0.explanation: Pull shifts work to read time; with feeds read far more often than posts are written, that means many queries per page load. Pull actually stores fewer copies than push.

hld-feed-chat:0.prompt: With fan-out on write, a user unfollows an account. What must happen to keep the feed correct?
options: Nothing; the timeline will naturally expire in 30 days
Delete the user's entire timeline and rebuild it from scratch every time
Remove (or filter at read time) that author's post ids from the user's precomputed timeline, and stop future fan-out to them
Block the author globally
hld-feed-chat:0.explanation: Precomputed timelines contain stale entries after an unfollow, so either clean them up asynchronously or filter by the current follow graph when reading. Full rebuilds on every unfollow are wasteful.

hld-feed-chat:0.prompt: Many users have accounts but haven't logged in for months. How should a push-based feed system treat them?
options: Skip fan-out to inactive users and build their timeline on demand (pull) when they next log in
Fan out to them like everyone else so their feed is instantly ready
Delete their accounts
Fan out only celebrity posts to them
hld-feed-chat:0.explanation: Writing into timelines nobody reads wastes most of the fan-out budget; lazily building on login trades a slower first load for a large saving. Fanning out to all inactive users spends writes and cache memory for nothing.

hld-feed-chat:0.prompt: Which statements about the hybrid push/pull feed model are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The celebrity threshold (e.g. followers > some N) is a tunable trade-off between write and read cost
Reads for a user who follows celebrities must merge their precomputed timeline with celebrities' recent posts
Celebrity posts become invisible to followers
Celebrities' recent posts can be cached heavily because many users read the same ones
The hybrid model needs no ranking or merge logic
hld-feed-chat:0.explanation: The threshold tunes the trade-off, reads merge pushed and pulled posts, and celebrity posts are hot so they cache well. Celebrity posts remain visible via the pull path, and merging at read time obviously needs merge/ranking logic.

hld-feed-chat:0.prompt: A celebrity posts and a fan-out queue backlog forms, delaying normal users' posts by minutes. Which mitigations make sense? Select all that apply.
options: Route celebrity accounts to the pull path so they never enter the fan-out queue
Use separate queues/worker pools so huge fan-outs don't block ordinary ones
Fan out to active followers first and inactive ones later (or never)
Process fan-out synchronously inside the post request
Shard fan-out work into batches of followers processed in parallel
hld-feed-chat:0.explanation: Pulling celebrities, isolating queues, prioritising active users and batching parallel work all reduce lag. Fanning out synchronously in the post request would make posting slow and fragile.

hld-feed-chat:0.prompt: Pure fan-out on write gives the lowest feed-read latency, because the timeline is already precomputed when the user opens the app.
options: True
False
hld-feed-chat:0.explanation: True. Reads become a single lookup of precomputed post ids (plus hydration). The price is write amplification and storage, which is why it's combined with pull for high-follower accounts.

hld-feed-chat:0.prompt: With fan-out on write, timelines typically store full post content (text, media) for each follower to avoid any further lookups.
options: True
False
hld-feed-chat:0.explanation: False. Timelines usually store only post ids (maybe with a score), and posts are hydrated from a post cache/store at read time. Copying full content per follower would multiply storage and make edits and deletes very costly.

hld-feed-chat:1.prompt: Which Redis data structure fits a per-user timeline of post ids ordered by time or score, trimmed to the latest 800 entries?
options: A Redis string holding a JSON array
A Redis set
A Redis sorted set (ZADD with score, ZREVRANGE to read, ZREMRANGEBYRANK to trim)
A Redis HyperLogLog
hld-feed-chat:1.explanation: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score with O(log N) inserts and range reads, and trimming by rank caps memory. A JSON string needs read-modify-write races; sets are unordered; HLL only counts.

hld-feed-chat:1.prompt: Why do feed systems cap cached timelines (e.g. only the latest few hundred post ids per user)?
options: Redis cannot hold more than 1,000 items per key
Most users only scroll recent items; capping bounds memory, and older pages can fall back to slower storage or pull
Ranking algorithms only work on 800 items
Users are not allowed to see older posts
hld-feed-chat:1.explanation: Memory cost scales with users × entries, while deep scrolling is rare, so caching only the head of each timeline is efficient. Redis sorted sets can hold far more; the cap is an economic choice.

hld-feed-chat:1.prompt: Timeline entries store post ids. What is 'hydration' in this context?
options: Fetching full post objects, author info and counts for the ids (usually via batched cache lookups) before returning the feed
Re-ranking the feed every second
Compressing the timeline
Replicating the timeline to another region
hld-feed-chat:1.explanation: The timeline gives ids; hydration batch-fetches post content, author profiles and engagement counts from caches (e.g. MGET) and the store. Doing it per id sequentially would cause many round trips.

hld-feed-chat:1.prompt: A feed API uses OFFSET-based pagination over a timeline that receives new posts constantly. Users see duplicate posts when loading page 2. Why, and what's the fix?
options: The cache is corrupt; flush it
OFFSET is too large; use smaller pages
Ranking is non-deterministic; disable ranking
New items shift positions between requests; use cursor pagination keyed on the last seen score/id
hld-feed-chat:1.explanation: With offsets, inserts at the top push items down, so page 2 repeats items from page 1. A cursor ('items with score below X, tiebreak by id') is stable under inserts. Smaller pages don't change the shifting problem.

hld-feed-chat:1.prompt: Moving from a chronological feed to a ranked feed, what is a common two-stage architecture?
options: Rank every post in the system for every request
Candidate generation (gather a few hundred to thousands of recent candidates from followees, interests) followed by a ranking model that scores and orders them
Sort only by like count
Let the client rank posts locally with all data
hld-feed-chat:1.explanation: Scoring everything is infeasible, so systems retrieve a manageable candidate set cheaply and then apply a heavier ranking model (engagement predictions, freshness, diversity). Pure like-count sorting ignores freshness and personalisation.

hld-feed-chat:1.prompt: The Redis cluster holding timelines loses a node and some users' cached timelines vanish. What should the read path do?
options: Return an empty feed until the next post arrives
Return HTTP 500 for those users
Rebuild the timeline on a cache miss by pulling recent posts from followees (with rate limiting to avoid a stampede), then repopulate the cache
Read every user's timeline from a nightly backup
hld-feed-chat:1.explanation: Timelines are a derived cache, so a miss should trigger a rebuild from the source of truth (follow graph + posts), throttled or coalesced to avoid overwhelming the post store. Empty feeds or errors are bad user experience for a recoverable situation.

hld-feed-chat:1.prompt: A ranked feed scores posts with engagement predictions. Why might it also apply rules like 'no more than 2 consecutive posts from the same author'?
options: Ranking models can't score posts from the same author
Redis sorted sets reject duplicate authors
It reduces storage
Pure score ordering can produce repetitive, low-diversity feeds; diversity and freshness re-ranking improves user experience and long-term engagement
hld-feed-chat:1.explanation: Score-only ranking can cluster one prolific author or topic. Post-ranking adjustments (diversity, freshness, dedup) balance short-term predicted engagement with feed quality. It's a product rule, not a storage constraint.

hld-feed-chat:1.prompt: Which signals are commonly used when ranking feed candidates? Select all that apply.
options: Post age (freshness decay)
Affinity between viewer and author (past interactions)
Predicted engagement (like, comment, share probability)
The author's database shard number
Content type preferences of the viewer (video vs text)
hld-feed-chat:1.explanation: Freshness, affinity, predicted engagement and content preferences are classic ranking features. A shard number is an infrastructure detail with no relevance to what the viewer wants.

hld-feed-chat:1.prompt: A viral post's like count is displayed in millions of feeds, and the counter row becomes a write hotspot. Which techniques help? Select all that apply.
options: Shard the counter into N sub-counters and sum them on read
Buffer increments in memory or Redis and flush aggregated deltas periodically
Show approximate counts (e.g. '1.2M') served from cache with a short TTL
Increment the same SQL row synchronously on every like with a row lock
Store each like as an event and count asynchronously
hld-feed-chat:1.explanation: Sharded counters, batched deltas, cached approximate display values and async event counting spread or defer writes. A synchronous locked update per like serialises all writers on one row, which is exactly the hotspot.

hld-feed-chat:1.prompt: In a ranked feed, using the ranking score alone as a pagination cursor can cause skipped or repeated posts if scores change between page loads.
options: True
False
hld-feed-chat:1.explanation: True. Scores shift as engagement changes, so 'score < X' can skip or repeat items. Systems often snapshot the ranked list per session (cache the ordered ids) and paginate over that snapshot.

hld-feed-chat:1.prompt: Because the timeline cache is a derived view, losing it means losing users' posts.
options: True
False
hld-feed-chat:1.explanation: False. Posts live in a durable store; the timeline cache only holds ids derived from the follow graph and posts, so it can be rebuilt. Losing it costs latency and rebuild load, not data.

hld-feed-chat:2.prompt: Why do chat apps like WhatsApp use persistent connections (e.g. WebSockets) rather than clients polling over HTTP?
options: WebSockets encrypt messages end-to-end automatically
HTTP cannot carry text messages
A persistent connection lets the server push messages instantly with low overhead, while polling adds latency and wastes requests when nothing is new
WebSockets don't need TCP
hld-feed-chat:2.explanation: Server push over a long-lived connection delivers messages in milliseconds without constant empty polls. WebSockets run over TCP and are not end-to-end encrypted by themselves (TLS only secures the hop; E2E needs something like the Signal protocol).

hld-feed-chat:2.prompt: Users' WebSocket connections are spread across 500 gateway servers. User A (on gateway 12) messages user B. How does the system know where to deliver?
options: Broadcast the message to all 500 gateways
A connection registry (e.g. Redis: userId → gatewayId) records which gateway holds each user's connection, and the message is routed there
User B polls every gateway
Always place A and B on the same gateway
hld-feed-chat:2.explanation: A registry maps user (or device) to gateway so a message is routed only to the right server, often via a per-gateway queue or pub/sub channel. Broadcasting to every gateway wastes work and doesn't scale.

hld-feed-chat:2.prompt: A gateway server crashes, dropping 100,000 connections. What happens to its entries in the connection registry if they were written without expiry?
options: Stale entries keep pointing users to a dead gateway, so messages are routed nowhere until cleaned up
Redis deletes them automatically when the gateway's TCP connection closes
Clients update the registry before disconnecting
Nothing; registries don't need cleanup
hld-feed-chat:2.explanation: A crashed server can't clean up, so entries need TTLs refreshed by heartbeats, plus delivery logic that treats a missing/dead target as 'offline, store for later'. Clients that lose connection can't write anything either.

hld-feed-chat:2.prompt: Each gateway holds ~500k idle WebSocket connections. What resource limits the number of connections per server most directly?
options: Disk space for each message
The number of CPU cores, since each connection needs its own thread
Database connection pool size
Memory per connection and OS limits like file descriptors (ulimit), plus kernel socket buffers
hld-feed-chat:2.explanation: Each socket uses a file descriptor and buffer memory, so fd limits and RAM dominate for mostly idle connections. Event-driven servers (Node.js, Netty, Erlang) don't need a thread per connection.

hld-feed-chat:2.prompt: A WebSocket gateway fleet sits behind a load balancer. You deploy a new gateway version. What is the key concern?
options: Messages are re-encrypted with a new key
Restarting a gateway drops all its connections; drain gradually and have clients reconnect with jittered backoff to avoid a reconnect storm
Load balancers don't support WebSockets
Users must reinstall the app
hld-feed-chat:2.explanation: Long-lived connections make deploys disruptive: a mass disconnect leads to everyone reconnecting at once. Rolling drains (close connections gradually with a reconnect hint) and client jitter spread the load. Modern L7 load balancers do support WebSockets.

hld-feed-chat:2.prompt: In a Node.js WebSocket gateway, what should the gateway do and NOT do?
options: Hold connections, authenticate, forward messages to backend services and push outbound messages; keep heavy business logic and storage in separate services
Run all chat business logic, including message storage, inside each gateway process
Store all message history in gateway memory
Run ranking models for each message
hld-feed-chat:2.explanation: Keeping gateways thin means they can be scaled and restarted independently of chat logic; durable storage and processing live behind them. Gateway memory is lost on restart and doesn't scale as a store.

hld-feed-chat:2.prompt: A user has the app open on a phone and on a laptop. How should the connection registry model this?
options: Store only the most recent connection and drop the other
Map userId → set of (deviceId, gatewayId) entries, each with its own TTL, and deliver to every active device
Reject the second login
Store one entry and let the phone forward messages to the laptop
hld-feed-chat:2.explanation: Multi-device support needs one registry entry per device connection; delivery fans out to all of them, and per-device TTLs handle individual disconnects. Keeping only the latest connection silently stops delivery to the other device.

hld-feed-chat:2.prompt: Which practices help keep WebSocket connections healthy at scale? Select all that apply.
options: Application-level heartbeats (ping/pong) to detect dead connections that TCP hasn't noticed
Client reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter
Authenticate on connect (e.g. a token in the handshake) and re-check on expiry
Open a new WebSocket for every message sent
Keep load-balancer idle timeouts longer than the heartbeat interval
hld-feed-chat:2.explanation: Heartbeats detect half-open connections, jittered reconnects avoid storms, handshake auth secures sessions, and idle timeouts above the heartbeat interval stop the LB from cutting healthy idle connections. Opening a socket per message defeats the purpose.

hld-feed-chat:2.prompt: Gateway A must hand a message to the gateway that holds the recipient's connection. Which inter-gateway routing approaches are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: Each gateway subscribes to its own Redis pub/sub channel or queue; senders publish to the target gateway's channel
Route via a message broker (e.g. Kafka partitioned by recipient, consumed by the owning gateway)
Gateways connect directly to each other over an internal RPC mesh using the registry
Write the message to a shared file that all gateways tail
Send every message to every gateway and let each filter
hld-feed-chat:2.explanation: Per-gateway pub/sub channels, a partitioned broker or direct RPC are all used in practice. Shared files don't scale or survive failures, and broadcasting to every gateway multiplies traffic by the fleet size.

hld-feed-chat:2.prompt: Pure Redis pub/sub is durable: if the target gateway is briefly disconnected, it receives the missed messages when it resubscribes.
options: True
False
hld-feed-chat:2.explanation: False. Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget; messages published while a subscriber is disconnected are lost. Durability must come from persisting messages first (message store, Redis Streams or Kafka) and syncing on reconnect.

hld-feed-chat:2.prompt: Server-Sent Events (SSE) can be a simpler alternative to WebSockets when the server only needs to push data to the client, such as live notifications.
options: True
False
hld-feed-chat:2.explanation: True. SSE is one-way server-to-client over plain HTTP with built-in reconnect and event ids. Chat needs frequent client-to-server messages too, which is why WebSockets are the usual choice there.

hld-feed-chat:3.prompt: Why shouldn't a chat system order messages within a conversation by each client's device timestamp?
options: Device timestamps use the wrong time zone
Timestamps can't be stored in databases
Device clocks are skewed or wrong, so messages could appear out of order; the server should assign a per-conversation sequence number
Clients don't have clocks
hld-feed-chat:3.explanation: Client clocks drift or are set manually, so ordering by them is unreliable. A server-assigned, monotonically increasing sequence per conversation gives one agreed order.

hld-feed-chat:3.prompt: What is the purpose of a client-generated message id (e.g. a UUID) on each sent chat message?
options: It replaces the server sequence number for ordering
It lets the server deduplicate retries, so a resend after a network glitch doesn't create a second copy
It encrypts the message
It identifies the recipient's device
hld-feed-chat:3.explanation: If the client times out waiting for an ack and resends, the server recognises the same client message id and returns the original ack instead of storing a duplicate. Ordering still comes from the server sequence.

hld-feed-chat:3.prompt: WhatsApp-style ticks show sent, delivered and read. What do these receipts correspond to?
options: Sent = server stored the message; delivered = recipient's device acknowledged receiving it; read = recipient opened the conversation
Sent = typed; delivered = server stored; read = recipient replied
All three are set together when the server stores the message
Sent = encrypted; delivered = decrypted; read = deleted
hld-feed-chat:3.explanation: The server ack gives 'sent', the recipient device's ack gives 'delivered', and a read event when the chat is viewed gives 'read'. Each is a separate event flowing back to the sender.

hld-feed-chat:3.prompt: A user comes back online after 3 days offline. How should the client catch up efficiently?
options: Download the user's entire message history again
Wait for each sender to resend
Poll each conversation every second until nothing new arrives
Send the last sequence number it has per conversation (or a global sync cursor); the server returns only newer messages, paginated
hld-feed-chat:3.explanation: Cursor-based sync transfers only the delta and is resumable if interrupted. Re-downloading everything wastes bandwidth, and senders shouldn't be responsible for re-delivery.

hld-feed-chat:3.prompt: A group chat with heavy traffic stores messages in Cassandra with partition key conversation_id and clustering key message sequence (descending). What does this design optimise?
options: Global full-text search across all chats
Fetching the latest N messages of one conversation with a single-partition, already-sorted read
Joins between messages and users
Counting unique senders across all conversations
hld-feed-chat:3.explanation: All of a conversation's messages live in one partition sorted by sequence, so 'latest 50' is a cheap slice. Very active conversations may also need time-bucketing in the partition key to keep partitions bounded. Cassandra doesn't do joins.

hld-feed-chat:3.prompt: How can a server assign increasing sequence numbers per conversation without one global counter becoming a bottleneck?
options: Use one global auto-increment across all conversations
Let each client pick its own sequence
Keep a counter per conversation (e.g. Redis INCR on conv:{id}:seq, or route each conversation to one owner that increments locally)
Use the current Unix time in seconds
hld-feed-chat:3.explanation: Ordering only matters within a conversation, so per-conversation counters spread load across keys/shards. A global counter serialises everything; client-chosen sequences conflict; second-resolution timestamps collide.

hld-feed-chat:3.prompt: A sender's message is stored and pushed to the recipient's gateway, but the recipient's phone loses network before acknowledging. What should the system do?
options: Mark it delivered anyway since it reached the gateway
Keep it as undelivered (in the recipient's pending/offline queue) and deliver it on reconnect sync; the client dedupes by message id
Delete the message
Ask the sender to resend manually
hld-feed-chat:3.explanation: Delivery is only confirmed by the device ack; until then the message stays pending and will be re-sent during sync, with dedup by id preventing duplicates. Treating the gateway push as delivered would lose messages.

hld-feed-chat:3.prompt: Which statements about message delivery guarantees in chat are correct? Select all that apply.
options: At-least-once delivery plus client-side dedup by message id gives effectively-once display
The server should persist a message before acknowledging 'sent' to the sender
Exactly-once network delivery is easy to guarantee with TCP alone
Per-conversation ordering is usually enough; global ordering across all chats is unnecessary
Read receipts must be delivered before the message itself
hld-feed-chat:3.explanation: Persist-then-ack, at-least-once with dedup and per-conversation ordering are the standard design. TCP only guarantees delivery within one connection and can't prevent app-level resends across reconnects, and receipts naturally come after messages.

hld-feed-chat:3.prompt: In a 1,000-member group chat, per-member read receipts become expensive. Which designs reduce cost? Select all that apply.
options: Store a per-member 'last read sequence' instead of a receipt row per message per member
Aggregate receipts and show counts or 'read by all' rather than pushing every individual receipt to every member
Batch and debounce receipt updates from clients
Send each read receipt to all 1,000 members immediately as it happens
Disable or limit detailed receipts above a group size threshold
hld-feed-chat:3.explanation: A last-read pointer per member replaces N×M receipt rows; aggregation, batching and size thresholds cut fan-out. Broadcasting every receipt to every member is O(members²) traffic per message read wave.

hld-feed-chat:3.prompt: If a server assigns sequence numbers per conversation, two messages sent at nearly the same moment by different members will still be shown in the same order on every member's device.
options: True
False
hld-feed-chat:3.explanation: True. The server sequence is the single source of order, so all clients sort by it and agree, even if the senders' perceived order differed. That consistency is the reason to use server-assigned sequences.

hld-feed-chat:3.prompt: Once a message is delivered to the recipient's device, the server must keep it forever in all chat designs.
options: True
False
hld-feed-chat:3.explanation: False. Some designs (classic WhatsApp) treat the server as a relay and delete messages after delivery, with history living on devices and backups; others (Slack, Telegram cloud chats) keep server-side history. It is a product and privacy trade-off.

hld-feed-chat:4.prompt: What is the simplest scalable way to track whether a user is online?
options: Write every keystroke to the database
Ask the user's contacts whether they can see the user
Run a SQL query over all open WebSocket connections
Clients send periodic heartbeats; the server sets a presence key with a short TTL (e.g. 30-60 s) that expires if heartbeats stop
hld-feed-chat:4.explanation: A TTL key refreshed by heartbeats naturally flips to offline when the client disappears, without needing a clean disconnect. Querying connections or writing per keystroke doesn't scale.

hld-feed-chat:4.prompt: Why rely on heartbeat expiry rather than only on WebSocket close events to mark users offline?
options: Close events are not part of the WebSocket protocol
When a phone loses network or the app is killed, no close frame is sent, so the server may not notice the disconnect for a long time
Heartbeats use less bandwidth than close events
Close events always arrive twice
hld-feed-chat:4.explanation: Abrupt disconnects (tunnels, airplane mode, crashes) leave half-open TCP connections with no close event, so a TTL/heartbeat timeout is needed. Clean close events can still be used to mark offline faster when they arrive.

hld-feed-chat:4.prompt: A user with 2,000 contacts flickers online/offline every few seconds on a weak mobile network. What problem does this cause, and what's a common fix?
options: It corrupts the message store; fix by disabling presence
Each transition fans out to all contacts, generating a flood of presence events; debounce transitions (e.g. only mark offline after a grace period)
It increases the user's battery usage only; no server fix needed
Contacts receive duplicate messages; fix with idempotency keys
hld-feed-chat:4.explanation: Presence changes fan out to every interested contact, so flapping multiplies traffic. A grace period before announcing 'offline' (and coalescing rapid changes) suppresses flicker. Message duplication is unrelated.

hld-feed-chat:4.prompt: For a user with 5,000 contacts, pushing every presence change to all contacts is expensive. Which approach reduces fan-out most effectively?
options: Push presence only to contacts who are currently online and actually viewing something that shows it (e.g. subscribed to that user's status while a chat or list is open)
Push presence changes to all contacts via SMS
Store presence in the database and let clients query it every second
Send presence once per day
hld-feed-chat:4.explanation: Subscription-based presence sends updates only to viewers who care right now, cutting most fan-out. Per-second polling by every client creates even more load, and daily updates make presence useless.

hld-feed-chat:4.prompt: How is 'last seen at 10:42' typically implemented alongside online presence?
options: Computed from the latest message the user sent
Stored only on the user's device
When the presence key expires or the user disconnects, record a durable last-seen timestamp (e.g. updated on heartbeat at a coarse interval)
Derived from the load balancer's access logs
hld-feed-chat:4.explanation: Online status lives in a short-TTL cache, while last-seen is persisted on disconnect (or periodically from heartbeats) so it survives the key expiring. Last message sent misses users who read without writing.

hld-feed-chat:4.prompt: Presence data lives in Redis with TTL keys. A Redis node fails and its presence keys are lost. How bad is this?
options: Very bad: message history is lost
Users can no longer log in
All messages to those users will be dropped permanently
Mostly cosmetic and self-healing: affected users briefly show offline until their next heartbeat recreates the key
hld-feed-chat:4.explanation: Presence is soft state continuously refreshed by heartbeats, so loss recovers within one heartbeat interval. That's why presence usually doesn't need durable, strongly consistent storage. Message delivery uses the connection registry and offline queue, not presence.

hld-feed-chat:4.prompt: What heartbeat interval trade-off do mobile chat apps face?
options: Shorter intervals make presence more accurate but drain battery and increase server load; longer intervals save resources but make presence stale
Shorter intervals always save battery
Interval has no effect on presence accuracy
Longer intervals require more server memory
hld-feed-chat:4.explanation: Frequent heartbeats keep the radio awake and multiply requests across millions of clients; infrequent ones delay offline detection. Apps pick a middle ground (tens of seconds) and use OS push when backgrounded.

hld-feed-chat:4.prompt: Which statements about presence systems are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Presence is typically eventually consistent: a few seconds of staleness is acceptable
Presence state is usually kept in memory/cache rather than a primary relational database
Presence must be strongly consistent across all regions before a message can be sent
Typing indicators are ephemeral events that generally don't need to be persisted
A user with multiple devices is online if any device is connected
hld-feed-chat:4.explanation: Presence is soft, ephemeral, cache-backed state aggregated across devices, and typing indicators are fire-and-forget. Sending messages never waits on presence; offline recipients simply get messages on sync.

hld-feed-chat:4.prompt: Presence updates for 100 million online users are overwhelming the system. Which optimisations are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: Batch presence updates and push them to clients in periodic digests instead of one event per change
Hide exact presence in large groups (show only for 1:1 chats or small groups)
Shard presence keys across a Redis cluster by user id
Write every heartbeat to a durable, replicated SQL table with fsync
Use a grace period to suppress short offline/online flaps
hld-feed-chat:4.explanation: Batching, limiting presence where it adds little value, sharding and flap suppression cut load. Persisting every heartbeat durably turns a cheap soft-state signal into a massive write workload.

hld-feed-chat:4.prompt: A presence key with a 30-second TTL refreshed by 10-second heartbeats tolerates a couple of missed heartbeats before the user shows as offline.
options: True
False
hld-feed-chat:4.explanation: True. With heartbeats at a third of the TTL, one or two lost heartbeats (brief network blips) don't flip the user offline; only about 30 s without any heartbeat does. Setting the TTL equal to the heartbeat interval would cause constant flapping.

hld-feed-chat:4.prompt: Presence should be fanned out to all of a user's contacts in real time, even those who are offline, so it's ready when they open the app.
options: True
False
hld-feed-chat:4.explanation: False. Offline contacts can't receive pushes, and queueing presence for them is wasted work since it would be stale anyway. When they come online, they fetch the current presence of the contacts they're viewing.
